etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English stranglen, from Old French estrangler, from Latin strangulō, strangulāre, from Ancient Greek στραγγαλόομαι (strangalóomai, “to be strangled”), from στραγγάλη (strangálē, “a halter”); compare στραγγός (strangós, “twisted”) and string. Displaced Middle English wirien, awurien (“to strangle”) (> English worry).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To kill someone by squeezing the throat so as to cut off the oxygen supply; to choke, suffocate or throttle.

quote.citation: 1936, Robert Frost, “The Vindictives”, in A Further Range:
quote.text: And his subjects wrung all they could wring / Out of temple and palace and store. / But when there seemed no more to bring, / His captors convicted the king / Of once having started a war, / And strangled the wretch with a string.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be killed by strangulation, or become strangled.
(intransitive) To be stifled, choked, or suffocated in any manner.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: Shall I not then be stifled in the vault, /  […]  And there die strangled ere my Romeo comes?

quote.citation: 1626, Ovid, “The Eighth Booke”, in George Sandys, transl., Ovid’s Metamorphosis Englished […], London:  […]  William Stansby, →OCLC, page 165:
quote.text: Her, vvhom his furie hath from earth exil'd, / And in the ſtrangling vvaters drencht his child;  […]An adjective use.

definitions.definition: (finance) A trading strategy using options, constructed through taking equal positions in a put and a call with different strike prices, such that there is a payoff if the underlying asset's value moves beyond the range of the two strike prices.
